assessment.title: C2 Level Assessment
assessment.description: A proficiency-level assessment of nuanced grammar, lexical precision, reading, listening, inference, pragmatics, rhetoric, source evaluation, and synthesis.
assessment.instructions: Complete all sections carefully. Listening passages may be played a maximum of two times. Many items require interpretation, inference, source evaluation, or subtle distinctions in meaning.

questions.prompt: Which sentence most naturally softens a present request?
questions.option_a: I was wondering whether you could help.
questions.explanation: Past progressive can soften a current request.

questions.prompt: The figures ___ be available tomorrow if validation finishes today.
questions.explanation: Should expresses expectation.

questions.prompt: She said the system would fail, and ___ it did.
questions.explanation: So it did confirms the prediction.

questions.prompt: Several researchers, three of ___ had worked abroad, joined the study.
questions.explanation: Quantifier + whom is the formal structure.

questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves uncertainty in 'The policy may help'?
questions.explanation: The possibility remains hedged.

questions.prompt: Choose the form emphasizing an ongoing prior expectation.
questions.explanation: Past perfect continuous highlights prior duration.

questions.prompt: I didn't expect the delay, and neither ___ my colleagues.
questions.explanation: Neither + auxiliary + subject.

questions.prompt: The findings are stronger than ___ of the pilot study.
questions.explanation: Those substitutes for plural findings.

questions.prompt: Which client-facing request is most appropriate?
questions.option_a: We would appreciate confirmation by Friday.
questions.explanation: The register is professional and formal.

questions.prompt: In 'Although the evidence is limited, the findings suggest a pattern,' what is the main clause?
questions.explanation: The although-clause is subordinate.

questions.prompt: Which reformulation preserves concession?
questions.option_a: Although the evidence was limited, the proposal was approved.
questions.option_b: Because the evidence was limited, the proposal was approved.
questions.explanation: The concessive relationship is maintained.

questions.prompt: Which statement about aspect is incorrect?
questions.option_b: Perfect forms can link time points.
questions.option_d: Every progressive form means an action is literally happening at that exact moment.
questions.explanation: Aspect has broader discourse functions.

questions.prompt: Which word best describes a limiting condition rather than a total barrier?
questions.explanation: Constraint is a limiting factor.

questions.prompt: If an idea gains traction, it...
questions.explanation: The metaphor means increasing acceptance.

questions.prompt: What is a rhetorical question mainly used for?
questions.option_a: Persuasive effect rather than information seeking
questions.explanation: Its function is rhetorical.

questions.prompt: 'Not exactly ideal' is usually an example of...
questions.explanation: It softens criticism.

questions.prompt: What problem can voluntary survey response create?
questions.explanation: Respondents may not represent the full population.

questions.prompt: What is synthesis?
questions.option_c: Listing sources separately with no comparison
questions.explanation: Synthesis establishes relationships among evidence.

questions.prompt: What can 'sort of' do in spoken discourse?
questions.explanation: It often softens or approximates.

questions.prompt: Which principle is most important in critical evaluation?
questions.option_a: Strong rhetoric does not guarantee strong evidence
questions.explanation: Style and evidential quality must be assessed separately.

questions.prompt: After a disastrous rollout, 'Well, that went brilliantly' is most likely...
questions.explanation: Context reverses the literal positive meaning.

questions.prompt: Why is 'When Alex spoke to Jordan, they were upset' potentially ambiguous?
questions.option_a: The pronoun reference may be unclear
questions.explanation: The pronoun may not identify the referent clearly.

questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves the stance of 'The evidence suggests a possible benefit'?
questions.option_a: The evidence points to a potential benefit.
questions.explanation: The cautious evidential force is retained.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation is strongest?
questions.option_a: The argument is persuasive, but the causal evidence supports only a narrower conclusion.
questions.option_b: The argument sounds sophisticated, so it must be true.
questions.explanation: It separates rhetoric from evidence.

passages.title: Evidence, Incentives, and Interpretation
passages.instructions: Read the text and answer the four questions.
passages.content_text: A widely cited industry report claims that organizations adopting automated workflow tools reduce administrative costs by an average of 30 percent. The figure is striking, but interpreting it requires care. Participating organizations volunteered to provide data and were already customers of the companies sponsoring the report. This does not invalidate the findings, but it raises questions about representativeness and incentive structures. In addition, the report compares costs before and after implementation without using a matched comparison group. Some of the reduction may therefore reflect broader organizational changes that happened at the same time. The authors acknowledge several of these limitations, though the executive summary presents the headline figure more confidently than the methodology section does. The most defensible conclusion is not that automation necessarily reduces costs by 30 percent, but that substantial savings are possible in some contexts and deserve further independent evaluation.

questions.prompt: What representativeness concern is raised?
questions.option_c: All participants were randomly selected from every sector
questions.option_d: The sample was global by law
questions.explanation: Volunteer customers may not represent all organizations.

questions.prompt: Why is causal interpretation limited?
questions.option_a: There was no matched comparison group
questions.explanation: Other simultaneous changes may explain part of the reduction.

questions.prompt: What tension exists within the report?
questions.option_a: The executive summary is more confident than the methodology warrants
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts presentation with methodological caution.

questions.prompt: What conclusion does the writer support?
questions.option_a: Savings are possible but need further independent evaluation
questions.option_c: The report proves no savings occur
questions.explanation: The conclusion is cautious and evidence-aligned.

passages.title: The Rhetoric of Urgency
passages.instructions: Read the text and answer the four questions.
passages.content_text: Calls for urgent action are common in public debate, and sometimes urgency is entirely justified. Yet urgency is also a rhetorical resource. A speaker who asks, 'If we do not act now, when will we?' frames delay as negligence rather than as one possible strategic choice. Similarly, describing a policy window as 'closing rapidly' may encourage audiences to focus on the cost of waiting while paying less attention to the cost of acting too quickly. None of this means that urgent arguments are dishonest. It means that readers should distinguish the evidence for urgency from the language used to create a sense of urgency. A strong case should survive that distinction. If the underlying evidence shows that delay would create substantial harm, then urgent rhetoric may simply reflect reality. If the evidence is weak, however, rhetorical force can make a fragile argument appear stronger than it is.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say urgency can be?
questions.option_a: Both a real condition and a rhetorical resource
questions.explanation: The passage makes that distinction.

questions.prompt: What effect can 'If we do not act now, when will we?' have?
questions.explanation: The rhetoric constrains how delay is perceived.

questions.prompt: What critical distinction does the writer recommend?
questions.option_a: Evidence for urgency vs language creating urgency
questions.explanation: That is the central evaluative distinction.

questions.prompt: When is urgent rhetoric most justified?
questions.option_a: When evidence shows delay would cause substantial harm
questions.explanation: Rhetoric should track evidence.

passages.title: A Nuanced Project Discussion
passages.instructions: Listen carefully. You may play the audio twice.
passages.audio_text: Well, I mean, I wouldn't say the pilot failed exactly. It did expose several issues we hadn't anticipated, particularly around training and access rights. Actually, let me put that differently. The technical platform performed more or less as expected; what didn't work was the assumption that teams could adapt without much support. So, yes, the pilot created disruption, but that's partly what a pilot is for. I'd be more worried if we'd learned nothing from it.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker evaluate the pilot?
questions.explanation: The speaker resists a binary success/failure interpretation.

questions.prompt: What does 'let me put that differently' signal?
questions.explanation: The speaker reformulates the previous statement.

questions.prompt: What failed more than the technology itself?
questions.option_a: The assumption that teams could adapt with little support
questions.explanation: The speaker distinguishes platform performance from organizational adaptation.

questions.prompt: What would worry the speaker more?
questions.explanation: The speaker values learning from disruption.

passages.title: Synthesizing Conflicting Evidence
passages.instructions: Listen carefully. You may play the audio twice.
passages.audio_text: The three studies don't point in exactly the same direction. The first reports a modest productivity increase, the second finds no overall change but better performance on focused tasks, and the third concentrates on employee satisfaction rather than output. Taken together, I don't think the evidence supports the claim that hybrid work is universally more productive. What it does suggest is that outcomes vary by task type and by how the arrangement is managed. So the sensible conclusion is narrower: hybrid work can be beneficial under some conditions, but the conditions matter.

questions.prompt: Do the studies fully agree?
questions.option_c: They all measure the same thing
questions.explanation: The speaker says they differ.

questions.prompt: What universal claim is rejected?
questions.option_a: Hybrid work is always more productive
questions.explanation: The evidence does not support universal superiority.

questions.prompt: What joint conclusion is supported?
questions.option_a: Benefits depend on conditions and task type
questions.explanation: The synthesis is conditional.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker treat conflicting evidence?
questions.option_a: Narrows the conclusion rather than ignoring differences
questions.option_b: Chooses one study and discards the rest
questions.explanation: This is strong synthesis practice.
